At the beginning of this chapter, we wanted to see how the fierce political struggle between the different Islamic parties and schools gradually became an intellectual struggle as well.
One of the clearest signs of this change appeared in Islamic law. Two main approaches began to take shape: the school of reasoned judgment and the school of hadith.

This division became increasingly clear and began to develop with some independence from the political conflict itself. The reason was that Islamic law was now facing new conditions created by the Arab conquests. Muslims were entering regions where social relations were very different from those they had known in Arabia when Islam first appeared. The conquests also forced the Islamic state to create new forms of organization.
Islamic law therefore faced a new task. It had to deal with situations that had not existed before and develop new rulings for them, while still preserving the spirit of its general principles.

This historical challenge showed just how necessary it was for law to develop as life itself developed. And it was only natural that people would differ over how far the law should change, just as they differed over change in the wider sense. In every age and every society, people have tended to divide according to their social positions between those who defend what already exists and those who seek to renew it.
This was precisely the basis of the division among those concerned with Islamic law.

The conservatives rejected rulings that had no explicit basis in the Qurʾan or the Sunna. The reformers, by contrast, used their own reasoned judgment to derive new rulings for questions that neither of these two main sources addressed. These questions had not existed in Arabian society when Islamic law first appeared. The reformers therefore used rational reasoning alongside the general principles of the law.
From this division came two schools. The first became known as the People of Reasoned Judgment (Ahl al-Raʾy), and the second as the People of Hadith (Ahl al-Ḥadīth).

The second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, had in practice stood on the side of reasoned judgment during his caliphate. He made a number of rulings on his own judgment, and these later formed some of the earliest foundations of the school of raʾy.

By the middle of the first Islamic century, this school had developed a clearer identity. It relied more heavily on independent judgment in matters of law and less heavily on hadith, especially after doubts had spread about the authenticity of many reports attributed to the Prophet.

The other, more conservative school reacted strongly against this position. Some of its members went beyond simply rejecting reasoned judgment and independent legal interpretation. They also went so far in their use of hadith that some of them placed hadith above Qurʾanic texts.
Even so, the school of reasoned judgment found many supporters in regions far from the Hijaz, where Islam had first appeared.
This division eventually spread beyond questions of law. It became a wider intellectual division over many of the new problems created by the development of Arab-Islamic society.

We therefore find many members of the school of reasoned judgment supporting an idea that emerged from the debate over divine decree and human action: the idea that human beings are free to choose their actions. Those who later became associated with this view were known as the Qadarites.

Many followers of the hadith school, by contrast, supported the opposite view. They denied human freedom and held that every human action, good or bad, comes from God. Human beings, in other words, act under God’s decree and predestination. Those who later became known for this view were called the Jabriyya, or the advocates of compulsion.

So each side in the legal debate—the conservatives on one side and the more forward-looking current on the other—moved naturally toward the side that best matched its outlook in this new intellectual struggle.

We also saw in this chapter that the development of Arab-Islamic society during the early Islamic period—the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the Umayyads—created the need for a broad cultural movement.

This movement laid the basic foundations for organizing the different kinds of knowledge connected with Islam. These included the language of the Qurʾan and hadith, their literary style, their legal and moral teachings, and questions of belief. They also included the history of Islam itself: its preaching, its conquests, its leading figures, and its relationship with pre-Islamic Arab life in language, literature, history, customs, and traditions.
Islam was the first and immediate starting point of this broad cultural movement.
But once the basic rules for organizing this knowledge had been created in response to the needs of Islam, those same rules became the starting point for a wider cultural revival.

Different branches of knowledge began to grow within it and gradually acquired some independence from one another. Each branch almost began to follow its own path. Their paths sometimes met, sometimes ran alongside one another, sometimes crossed, and sometimes joined together for a time before separating again.
They continued to borrow from one another—material, examples, methods, and teaching practices—but this did not remove the relative independence that each field gradually developed.
This independence did not become fully clear until the end of the second Islamic century.

In this way there emerged what came to be known as the “Arabic sciences”: language, grammar, rhetoric, history, biography, Qurʾanic interpretation, hadith, and the study of the transmitters of hadith. Then came the sciences connected with poetry: metre, rhyme, classifications of poets, comparisons between them, the transmission of poetry, commentaries on poetry, and so on.
One important feature in the history of these sciences is the way their relationship with Islam gradually changed.
At first, they were tied to Islam mainly as a religion. Over time, however, they became connected with Islam as a whole system for organizing public life.

This is why we argued in the chapter that the rise of these sciences was an important stage in the wider process of social development. They expressed the need for an organized body of knowledge suited to the new economic, social, administrative, and financial structures that were beginning to emerge under the Umayyad state.

They also served the needs created by the continued expansion of the Arab conquests. The conquered lands had to come to terms with the language of the conquerors, together with its literary, rhetorical, and legal meanings.
The development of society and culture also raised new intellectual questions, especially among people involved in the different fields of knowledge.
Some of these questions took a religious form and concerned matters of faith. Others became more theoretical and began to approach philosophical thought.

At the same time, growing social and cultural contact between the Arabs and other peoples, as well as with older civilizations, brought new ideas and new forms of practical experience into these debates.

The social order under the Umayyads, and especially its political structure, also strengthened the connection between these intellectual questions and the social conditions from which they had emerged.
The translation of older cultures into Arabic gradually expanded and eventually became an essential part of Arab cultural life.

Before this came what historians have called the movement of writing and compilation. This marked a major change. Culture moved from an earlier stage based mainly on oral accounts, transmission, and listening into a new stage based on writing, authorship, and reading.

This change helped the growing cultural exchange between the Arabs and other peoples. It also allowed the young Arabic sciences, which had until then been concerned largely with questions of form, to come into contact with new sciences that dealt more directly with subject matter and followed either an abstract rational approach or an experimental scientific one.
The centres of this cultural and scientific activity did not remain fixed. They shifted between cities and capitals as the centres of political conflict themselves shifted.
There were Mecca and Medina in the Hijaz. There were Basra and Kufa in Iraq before the rise of Baghdad. There was Damascus in Syria, and Fusṭāṭ—present-day Cairo—in Egypt.

But Basra and Kufa remained the most important and stable centres for a long time. This continued even when Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, and even after Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid caliphate and the main centre of cultural life.
In the third part of this chapter, we examined the earliest signs of philosophical thinking about questions of religious belief.

We began by discussing the views of a number of Western and Eastern scholars, both earlier and modern, who tried to identify the sources responsible for the appearance of these first philosophical tendencies in Arab-Islamic thought.

From this extended discussion, we reached the conclusion that the movement of Arab-Islamic thought toward rational and philosophical inquiry cannot be explained only by outside influences—Greek, Persian, Indian, or Christian.

There were also social, political, and Islamic religious roots within Arab-Islamic society itself. These internal forces helped produce the movement toward rational thought, sometimes directly and sometimes indirectly.
This does not mean denying the great influence of those outside sources.

Our point is more precise: outside influences entered a process of transformation within the internal struggles of Arab-Islamic society. These struggles might take a religious and sectarian form, or a social and political one.

By the second half of the first Islamic century, these conflicts were increasingly turning into forms of intellectual struggle. Someone looking only at the surface might imagine that these intellectual debates existed on their own, separate from what was actually happening within society and from the laws governing its historical development at the time.

In examining this intellectual change, we found that one basic question stood at the centre of almost all its different currents: the problem of divine decree and predestination, and its relationship to human action and human responsibility.
Historically, this question took on a particularly important form and became known as the problem of compulsion and free choice.
The debate centred on a simple question: Are human beings compelled to act as they do, or do they choose their actions freely?

In other words, do people have freedom of will and choice in the good and evil they do? Or are they subject in all things to the absolute will of God, so that everything decreed and predestined, good or bad, comes from God?
Later scholars described this as the question that set all Arab thought in motion during that period.

This description fits the historical reality very closely. From the moment the issue appeared as an intellectual problem during the early Umayyad period in the East, it became a central dividing line in intellectual, religious, social, and political conflict.
Because this question played such a major historical and intellectual role, we had to give it more space than any other issue in the chapter.
We divided our discussion into four main parts:
B — Its social and political roots
A — The Historical Origins of the Problem of Predestination

Our investigation showed that predestination became an intellectual problem connected with human responsibility sometime between the first and second halves of the first Islamic century. This conclusion is based on reliable sources in the history of Islamic schools and sects.
But people had discussed the question earlier on a purely religious level.

The Prophet and the first generation of his Companions had spoken about it, and ordinary people had asked the Rightly Guided Caliphs and other Companions how far divine decree and predestination governed human actions.

From this historical background, we concluded that the problem was not simply invented by the three thinkers who later became famous for defending human freedom and denying that divine predestination controls the human will.
These three men were Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ. All three were killed for political reasons in connection with the ideas they defended.

The problem already existed independently of them. People were discussing it, asking questions about it, and struggling to find an answer that would satisfy both their reason and their religious faith.
What these three early defenders of free will achieved, together with their teacher al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, was to give this already existing problem its first clear intellectual form.
They also took what we regard as its positive and progressive side.
And they defended their ideas with remarkable courage and commitment—so much so that they ultimately died for them.
B — Its Social and Political Roots

Our discussion of the social and political roots of the problem was deliberately extensive. We wanted to look at it from different angles and examine the historical events, patterns, and evidence themselves before drawing a conclusion that we believe comes close to the truth.
This required us to discuss the views and conclusions of a number of modern and contemporary scholars.

Through that discussion, we tried to strengthen the position we had reached: that the problem of predestination did not appear in Umayyad society simply as an intellectual phenomenon isolated from the intense social and political conflicts of that society.
For the same reason, it cannot be explained simply as the result of outside intellectual, philosophical, or religious influences coming from Greek culture, Persian culture, or Christian theology.
Those influences did play a part, but mainly by helping shape the first intellectual formulations of the problem.

We based our position on historical events, patterns, texts, and other materials that we were able to find in the main sources dealing with this stage in the development of Arab-Islamic society, between the second half of the seventh century and the first half of the eighth century CE.
